notes.title: Intro phase — spec
notes.body:
TIME
  1 real second = 1 in-game minute. The working day runs 07:00 to midnight —
  1,020 real seconds, seventeen minutes. Night is skipped or fast-forwarded.
  (Current code: dayLengthSeconds 240 for a full 24 h. Needs changing.)

  The long day is deliberate and stays long. It is thinking room: time to drive
  about, look at things, and later to pull an assembly line apart and rebuild it
  without a new quota landing every five minutes. It is not meant to be filled
  with work.

THE LOOP
  Right-click a crate, right-click the mark in the trailer, hit the plate to
  send the truck. Trucks do not leave on their own — that is an upgrade.

PACING — each unlock adds a source of action, and the player chooses the pace
  · First truck sent          -> the shop opens
  · First charge point bought -> the first boat is allowed to arrive
  · Then queue length, then per-bot automation, then a second bot
  Someone who wants to keep busy always has a new thing; someone who wants to
  potter about can.

WHAT THE INTRO DOES NOT DO
  It does not end with a clear floor. The 1x2s, the 2x2s and the steel all
  need upgrades that arrive later, so a good deal of cargo is still sitting
  there when the factory phase starts. That is intentional: you plan the first
  factory around the crates you cannot move yet, and clearing them later buys
  you floor space and a better layout. Floor space becomes a resource.

QUEUE
  Starts at length 0 — one order at a time. Bought up a step at a time, and
  deliberately NOT the first purchase: charging comes first, then queue, then
  per-bot automation, so the player buys a bot, automates it and watches it work.

  The queue must not become vestigial once bots are automatic. Its long-term
  home is player-authored routes in the factory phase — drawn paths through an
  assembly line, rather than bots only ever choosing for themselves.

CHARGING
  Every charge point sealed at the start. The first purchase is a charge point.
  Charging costs money by the amount drawn, subject to the no-lock rules.

notes.title: No game over — how the intro avoids a hard lock
notes.body:
The intro has to teach that power runs out and costs money, without ever
leaving a player unable to continue. The failure it must never allow: flat bot,
empty floor, no money.

Proposed rules, all cheap to implement:

· RESERVE FLOOR. A bot never drops fully to zero. It keeps a small reserve —
  enough to crawl and to reach a pad. Low power still refuses to lift, so the
  lesson lands, but the bot is never immobile.

· THE BOAT WAITS. No boat arrives until the first charge point is bought. You
  cannot be given more work than you have the power to do.

· CHARGING CANNOT BANKRUPT YOU. Power is billed by the amount drawn, but if you
  cannot pay, you get charged anyway and the meter simply does not run. The
  cost is real when you have money and invisible when you do not. This keeps the
  mechanic without ever being the thing that ends a run.

· MISSING A QUOTA COSTS SOMETHING, NOT EVERYTHING. A fine, a docked payment, a
  reputation hit. Never a run ending.

Together these mean there is no state the player can reach that has no way out,
which is what an incremental should guarantee. The pressure comes from wanting
to go faster, not from the threat of losing.

notes.title: Open decisions before building the intro
notes.body:
SETTLED

1. Capability is TWO independent axes, both per-bot, both upgradeable:
   · Size — how big a footprint the deck takes, and therefore how many crates:
     1x1 -> 1x2 (or two 1x1) -> 2x2 (or two 1x2, or four 1x1).
   · Weight — timber only -> steel as well.
   They stack, so a 1x1 heavy hauler is a legitimate build. Steel is the most
   expensive line and is meant to stay out of reach longest, but a player may
   choose to buy into it early and stay small.

2. No game over at all. See the separate no-lock note.

3. The first boat arrives after the first truck or two, on day one.

4. Quota is typed and dynamic from the start, even while it is always crates.

STILL OPEN

5. Price of a full charge, and whether it is billed at all during the intro.
6. Whether night 00:00-07:00 fast-forwards, cuts, or is a scored end-of-day.
7. Day-one quota size.

notes.title: Design feedback — what works and what I would watch
notes.body:
WHAT IS STRONG

· Boat as faucet, truck as sink. This is a real two-sided loop and it finally
  gives the water dock a job. The starting mess being a one-off and the boat
  being the ongoing supply is a clean story: the intro is "clear the building",
  the game is "work the port".
· The shop as a physical room solves the per-bot upgrade targeting problem for
  free. The bot on the plate is the bot upgraded.
· Freezing both the clock AND the factory in the shop is the right call. The
  drive there and back is the cost.
· Queue starting at zero. Correct. Teach one thing at a time.

WHAT I WOULD WATCH

1. THE BIGGEST RISK: the least automated phase is first.
   Every incremental that front-loads manual work loses people in the first
   twenty minutes. The pleasure of the genre is watching the machine run, not
   being the machine. Auto-pickup should arrive far earlier than instinct says
   — inside the first hour of play, not as a mid-game reward.

2. Seventeen-minute days versus a twelve-crate quota.
   A round trip is about twenty seconds, so a day holds roughly fifty crates.
   A quota of twelve is done in four minutes, leaving thirteen minutes of
   nothing. Either the quota fills most of the day, or the early days are
   shorter. Dead air teaches the player the game is slow.

3. The floor runs out before the boats arrive.
   Twenty-nine liftable crates on the floor, twenty-four slots in a trailer.
   Day one at quota twelve leaves seventeen; day two clears it. Boats need to
   start by day two or three, not after the intro ends. Introducing the water
   early is also just better — it is the most distinctive thing in the building.

4. One hard loss in a seventeen-minute intro is expensive.
   Consider making the FIRST miss scripted and survivable (a fine, a warning, a
   docked payment) with the real game-over on the second, even in the intro.
   The lesson lands either way; the restart does not cost seventeen minutes.

5. Tune the electricity price deliberately.
   A crate costs 0.0245 of a charge and sells for $45. For power to be a real
   but not crushing cost — say 10-20% of revenue — a full charge should be
   roughly $200-360. Worth choosing rather than discovering.

6. Speed upgrades do not reduce energy per crate, and that is good.
   Drain is per DISTANCE, not per second, so going faster costs the same charge.
   Route length and efficiency are the energy levers; speed is the time lever.
   Two clean, separate axes. Keep it that way.

7. Make the quota typed from day one.
   Even while it is always "12 timber crates", store it as a list of
   (item, count). Retrofitting item types into a crate counter later is
   expensive; designing it in now is free.

8. Per-bot upgrades get awkward around a dozen bots.
   "New bots ship with what you own" needs to arrive before the fleet is big
   enough for shopping trips to be a chore. A retrofit-all option too.

9. Night is free tension.
   The board going amber as the day runs out is a deadline signal that costs no
   new systems and uses the day cycle you already have.

notes.title: Game shape — the whole arc
notes.body:
The game is a long chain of phases. Each one shifts what the player is
managing, while keeping everything from the previous phase alive to go back and
optimise. Nothing is ever taken away; every phase is more advanced than the last.

1. INTRO — clear the abandoned warehouse.
   One manual robot, crates all over the floor, a daily quota. Teaches movement,
   the order queue, that cargo differs, the battery, and selling. Ends when the
   floor is clear.

2. THE PORT — boats supply, trucks ship.
   A flatbed boat berths between the indents in the water dock and extends
   boarding platforms. Bots board it and take crates off. It leaves when it is
   empty and no bot is aboard; a new one comes later. Fast work means more boats
   per day. This is what replaces the finite starting stock, and it is the first
   ongoing loop.

3. THE FACTORY — open crates for components, assemble goods, sell for more.
   Forced by the quota starting to demand built items rather than raw crates.

4. MULTIPLE SITES — buy adjacent warehouses, bots travel between them, sites
   supply each other.

5. BEYOND — seafloor, space. Thousands of bots.

6. PRESTIGE — not designed yet.

The through-line is bots: getting them, upgrading them, and eventually watching
them work without you.

notes.title: Upgrade catalogue 5 — additions
notes.body:
Added after the first pass.

75. Battery chemistry — a flat percentage more capacity, repeatable, cheap
    early and steeply priced later.
76. Charge threshold tuning — set the level at which auto-charge triggers, so a
    fleet can be biased towards uptime or towards fewer trips.
77. Idle shutdown — a parked bot draws almost nothing, removing the overnight
    drain on a fleet that is not working.
78. Battery health — capacity stops decaying with cycle count (only if decay is
    ever introduced; do not add decay just to sell the cure).
79. Swap packs — instead of charging in place, a bot exchanges its pack at a
    point in seconds, and the pack recharges on the rack.
80. Programmed routes — the player draws a path and a bot follows it as a
    standing order. The long-term home of the queue system once bots pick their
    own jobs, and the natural interface for an assembly line.
81. Route sharing — assign one drawn route to several bots at once.
82. New bot chassis types beyond the hauler. Flying and water bots are already
    planned much later; the hauler should not be assumed to be the only ground
    frame either — a small fast courier and a slow high-capacity mover are two
    obvious ground variants that trade against each other.

notes.title: Upgrade catalogue 1 — the bot itself (per-bot)
notes.body:
Per-bot unless marked. Bought by standing THAT bot on the plate.

 1. Deck I — takes a 1x2, or two 1x1 side by side.
 2. Deck II — takes a 2x2, or two 1x2, or four 1x1.
 3. Heavy lift — steel, at whatever deck size the bot already has.
 4. Speed I / II / III.
 5. Agility — faster turning, so short repositioning stops being the slow part.
 6. Battery capacity — a longer shift between charges.
 7. Charge rate — fills faster on a pad, so pads serve more bots.
 8. Drive efficiency — less charge per metre travelled.
 9. Arm speed — shortens the grab and set-down cycle.
10. Regenerative braking — recovers a trickle when slowing down.
11. Deep reserve — keeps working below the normal flat threshold.
12. Load stabiliser — no speed penalty for turning with a crate aboard.
13. Twin deck — stack two crates vertically on one bot.
14. Reinforced tracks — ignores the floor-condition speed penalty, if one exists.

notes.title: Upgrade catalogue 2 — autonomy and the fleet
notes.body:
AUTONOMY (per-bot)
15. Queue length +1. Repeatable. Starts at 0.
16. Auto-pickup — finds the nearest crate it is rated for, collects it, stops.
17. Auto-deliver — takes what it is holding to an available trailer.
18. Auto-charge — returns to a pad below a threshold, on its own.
19. Loop orders — repeats its queue forever instead of ending idle.
20. Zone assignment — only works crates inside an area you mark out.
21. Selection rule — nearest / highest value / longest sitting there.
22. Boat handling — will board a berthed boat and work it.
23. Truck dispatch — hits the plate itself once the trailer is full.
24. Home berth — returns to a chosen spot when it has nothing to do.
25. Traffic sense — better mutual avoidance, matters only in crowds.

FLEET (global)
26. Buy a bot.
27. Bot bay — raises the fleet cap.
28. Standard issue — new bots arrive with the upgrades you already own.
29. Retrofit — apply a per-bot upgrade to the whole fleet at a discount.
30. Shift rota — bots stagger charging so the fleet is never all on the pads.

notes.title: Upgrade catalogue 3 — power, dock and water
notes.body:
POWER
31. Charge point. Repeatable, unlocking bottom-up. The first purchase in the game.
32. Fast pad — higher rate, higher price per unit drawn.
33. Roof array — a share of daytime charging is free.
34. Off-peak tariff — power is cheaper at night.
35. Battery bank — store cheap night power to spend by day.
36. Charging rail — a strip of floor that trickles charge while driving over it.

DOCK AND SHIPPING
37. Unlock delivery dock 2 / 3 / 4.
38. Auto-dispatch — the truck leaves when full without the plate.
39. Quick turnaround — shortens the gap before the next trailer.
40. Long trailer — more slots.
41. Express contract — pays more, but must be filled before a deadline.
42. Freight terms — a flat percentage on every crate value.
43. Sorted loads — a bonus when a trailer goes out sorted by kind.
44. Second plate — dispatch a bay from either side of it.

WATER
45. Unlock the water dock.
46. Manifest — see what a boat is carrying before it berths.
47. Shorter gaps between boats.
48. Bigger boat.
49. Crane — lifts cargo off the boat onto the floor without a bot boarding.
50. Extra ramps — several bots can work one boat at once.
51. Salvage rights — occasional high-value crate in a load.

notes.title: Upgrade catalogue 4 — floor, economy, information
notes.body:
THE BUILDING
52. Lane markings — bots move faster along marked routes.
53. Staging area — a marked drop zone near the docks, halving the long trips.
54. Racking — crates stack, freeing floor.
55. Clear a column — opens up the aisles.
56. Buy the adjacent warehouse.
57. Floor resurfacing.

ECONOMY
58. Quota negotiation — buy the day's requirement down.
59. Grace day — bank one met quota against a future miss.
60. Insurance — a miss costs money instead of a life.
61. Contract — opt into a bigger quota for a bigger payout.
62. Market board — crate prices move; a readout shows when to hold.
63. Full-load bonus — a full trailer pays more per crate than a part load.
64. Reputation — streaks unlock better contracts.

INFORMATION (all diegetic, no HUD)
65. Board expansion — extra readouts: fleet charge, crates left, time to quota.
66. Floor beacons — marks crates nothing is assigned to.
67. Bay indicator — trailer fill visible from across the hall.
68. Water sign — boat ETA at the dock.

LATER PHASES (noted, not costed)
69. Crate opening and component extraction.
70. Assembly machines.
71. Component logistics between machines.
72. Site-to-site links.
73. Seafloor, space.
74. Prestige.

Water noise scale rule: repeat = 1/scale world units, feature = repeat/lattice (lattices 11/23/47/89). For ~20-unit features use scales around 0.0005-0.002. Scales near 0.02-0.14 sample sub-pixel and produce static.

Renderer architecture settled: raw WebGL2, 4-pass (albedo -> light -> composite -> glow -> overlay), one neutral bake with all time-of-day from the lighting pass. Measured ~26k robots @30fps vs 1750 in the Canvas2D concept.

tasks.title: Loading dock top-right: black truck curtain normally; when a truck is docked show its interior only, with fog of war elsewhere outside the warehouse
Fog of war outside the warehouse shell
Restock the floor, or the game ends after one truck
tasks.body:
29 liftable crates on the floor, 24 slots in a trailer, nothing
restocks. One full load and the game stalls with 5 crates left and a trailer
that can never fill.

Fixed by the boat (phase 2), which needs to arrive during the intro rather than
after it. Until then the floor could simply start fuller.

tasks.title: Day length: 1 real second = 1 in-game minute, 07:00 to midnight
tasks.body:
dayLengthSeconds is 240 for a full 24 h. The spec is 1,440 s for 24 h,
with play running 07:00-24:00 (1,020 s) and the night skipped or accelerated.
Decide which before wiring it, since the clock drives trailer return times.

tasks.title: Queue length becomes a purchased stat starting at 0
tasks.body:
Shift-right-click currently queues without limit. Make maximum queue
length a per-bot stat, zero at the start, bought one step at a time. Orders
beyond the limit are refused with the refusal sound.

tasks.title: Typed quota: a list of (item, count), not a crate counter
tasks.body:
Even while it is always '12 timber crates'. The factory phase needs the
quota to demand built items, and retrofitting item types into a plain counter
later is expensive. Free to design in now.

tasks.title: The shop room: drive in, buy by standing on a plate
tasks.body:
A door beside or under the display boards. Driving a bot in freezes the
clock AND the factory, and stops battery drain. Purchases are made by standing
a bot on a pressure plate — which also decides which bot receives a per-bot
upgrade, with no selection UI. Opens when the first daily quota is delivered.

tasks.title: Wire the rate model into the background clock
tasks.body:
src/sim/rateModel.ts is built and tested but not connected. MAX_CATCH_UP
becomes the boundary where live replay hands over to projection.

Two traps from the model's own notes: pass the load point as the MIDDLE of the
slot run (slot 0 is 6 m deeper into the bay and makes projections a fifth too
slow), and never let a projection touch ledger.avgSeconds.

tasks.title: Two-axis hauler capability: size and weight, both per-bot
tasks.body:
DECIDED: two independent, stacking axes, replacing the single
HaulerClass enum.

· Size: 1x1 -> 1x2 (or two 1x1) -> 2x2 (or two 1x2, or four 1x1)
· Weight: timber -> steel

Fixes a live bug as a side effect: steel 1x2 and steel 2x2 are currently
liftable by nothing, because liftRefusal in src/sim/cargo.ts demands Heavy for
the material AND Long-or-Big for the shape, and no single class is both.

Steel is the most expensive line and should stay out of reach longest, but a
1x1 heavy hauler must be a legal build — the axes are independent, not a ladder.

Deck capacity by size also needs modelling: a bot is not carrying 'a crate' any
more, it is carrying a set of crates that fit its deck.

tasks.title: No-lock guarantees: reserve floor, held boat, unbillable charge
tasks.body:
There is no game over. Implement the three guarantees from the no-lock
note:

1. A bot never reaches zero charge — it keeps a reserve that still allows the
   low-power crawl. Lifting is still refused in low power.
2. No boat arrives until the first charge point is bought.
3. Charging is billed only when the money exists; when it does not, the charge
   still happens and the meter does not run.

Missing a quota costs money or reputation, never the run.

tasks.title: Auto-charge: bots take themselves to a free pad when low
tasks.body:
Per-bot upgrade. Below a threshold, and only if a commissioned point is
free, the bot breaks off, docks, charges and resumes. Needs a claim on the pad
so two bots do not head for the same one.
